site.name: Alpine Ascents
site.tagline: A field guide to moving higher, smarter, and safer.
site.notice: Mountain travel is serious business. Treat this guide as an educational starting point, not a replacement for hands-on training, local forecasts, guide advice, or rescue guidance.

style.name: Alpine mountaineering
style.description: A fast, self-reliant style that links snow, ice and rock in one continuous mountain route. Conditions and decisions can change quickly.

style.name: Expedition climbing
style.description: Longer journeys that may use camps, acclimatization rotations, fixed lines and a larger logistics plan for remote or high-altitude terrain.

style.name: Rock & mixed climbing
style.description: Technical movement on rock, or on routes that combine rock, snow and ice. Protection, route-finding and partner communication are central.

style.name: Ice climbing
style.description: Climbing frozen waterfalls and alpine ice using specialist tools, crampons and protection. Ice quality and temperature can change the risk profile.

style.name: Ski mountaineering
style.description: Combines uphill travel on skis with mountain route-finding and descents. Avalanche education and terrain choices are essential.

style.name: Mountaineering trekking
style.description: Non-technical or lightly technical journeys at altitude that build endurance, mountain awareness and experience for bigger objectives.

record.label: Mount Everest
record.detail: World’s highest mountain above sea level; official height jointly announced by Nepal and China in 2020.

record.label: K2
record.detail: Second-highest mountain on Earth and famed for its demanding terrain and conditions.

record.label: Denali
record.detail: Highest mountain in North America, rising sharply above the Alaskan landscape.

record.label: Mont Blanc first ascent
record.detail: Jacques Balmat and Michel-Gabriel Paccard made the first recorded ascent on 8 August 1786.

record.label: Everest first ascent
record.detail: Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary reached Everest’s summit on 29 May 1953.

record.label: K2 first ascent
record.detail: Achille Compagnoni and Lino Lacedelli reached K2’s summit on 31 July 1954.

club.name: American Alpine Club
club.description: Community, education, publications, grants and resources for climbers and alpinists.

club.name: The Alpine Club
club.description: One of the world’s historic mountaineering clubs, supporting alpine knowledge and community.

club.name: Club Alpino Italiano
club.description: A national network supporting mountain culture, trails, huts, training and mountain protection.

club.name: Nepal Mountaineering Association
club.description: Supports Nepal’s mountaineering community, training, mountain stewardship and climbing culture.

club.name: New Zealand Alpine Club
club.description: A member-led club sharing climbing education, hut access, local knowledge and mountain community.

club.name: British Mountaineering Council
club.description: Climbing and hill-walking advice, access guidance, training resources and community support.

story.title: A new chapter in alpinism
story.description: Jacques Balmat and Michel-Gabriel Paccard’s ascent became a landmark in the development of modern mountaineering, inspiring generations to study routes, conditions and mountain science.

story.title: A team reaches the roof of the world
story.description: Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary reached the summit on 29 May 1953 after a carefully supported expedition. The achievement reflects teamwork, logistics, acclimatization and local expertise.

story.title: Persistence on a formidable peak
story.description: Achille Compagnoni and Lino Lacedelli reached the summit on 31 July 1954. K2 remains a reminder that high-altitude objectives demand conservative decisions and serious preparation.

fieldNote.title: Initial Kalymnos inspection findings
fieldNote.summary: The UIAA newsroom reports initial inspection findings linked to bolting and safety on Kalymnos. Follow the federation’s full updates and current equipment guidance before relying on fixed anchors or route hardware.

fieldNote.title: Fire risk in the 2026 State of the Mountains Report
fieldNote.summary: The UIAA highlighted fires as a focus of the 2026 State of the Mountains Report. Mountain stewardship includes understanding local wildfire restrictions, closures and changing seasonal conditions.

fieldNote.title: Safety standards continue to evolve
fieldNote.summary: The UIAA Safety Commission reported ongoing work on harnesses for rental use, ski-mountaineering helmet standards and rock-anchor performance. Check current standards and manufacturer notices before every trip.

fieldNote.title: UIAA Standard 110 for static ropes
fieldNote.summary: The UIAA announced its Static Ropes standard after a multi-year development process. Equipment labels and intended use matter: choose ropes for the system and context specified by the manufacturer.

fieldNote.title: AI-assisted avalanche incident analysis
fieldNote.summary: A mountain-operations article describes the use of AI-based methods to examine avalanche accident sequences and recurring decision-making patterns. It complements, rather than replaces, formal avalanche education and local bulletins.

galleryItem.title: First light on the high ridge
galleryItem.description: A visual reminder that alpine conditions can change quickly; plan the whole route, not just the summit photo.

galleryItem.title: Mountain safety & equipment standards
galleryItem.description: Browse current safety resources and climbing education from the UIAA.

galleryItem.title: Alpine skills: crampons, ice axe & movement
galleryItem.description: Find instructional demonstrations, then practise essential skills with a qualified instructor on suitable terrain.

guideline.title: Plan the route and the turnaround
guideline.text: Choose an objective that fits the least experienced team member, check access rules and set a turnaround time before leaving.

guideline.title: Read authoritative forecasts
guideline.text: Review mountain weather, avalanche bulletins, recent reports and local closures. Reassess if conditions differ from the plan.

guideline.title: Build skills before committing
guideline.text: Get hands-on instruction in navigation, rope systems, crampon and ice-axe use, crevasse rescue and emergency response as appropriate.

guideline.title: Carry and know your equipment
guideline.text: Inspect PPE, carry suitable insulation, food, water, navigation and emergency supplies, and practise with the equipment you plan to use.

guideline.title: Manage altitude and fatigue
guideline.text: Ascend gradually, recognise altitude-illness symptoms, communicate honestly about how the team feels and descend when symptoms warrant it.

guideline.title: Protect the mountain environment
guideline.text: Follow local regulations, minimise waste, respect wildlife and cultures, avoid damaging vegetation, and use established huts or camps responsibly.
